item.title: Ford Foundation Appoints Fatima Goss Graves to Board of Trustees
item.description:
• News and press
  • |News

NEW YORK – Today, the Ford Foundation announced the election of Fatima Goss Graves to its board of trustees. Ms. Goss Graves is the president and chief executive officer of the National Women’s Law Center and president of the National Women’s Law Center Action Fund. 

“We are thrilled to welcome Fatima Goss Graves’s perspective and expertise to the Ford Foundation Board of Trustees,” said Ursula Burns, Chair of the Ford Foundation Board of Trustees. “Fatima’s track record speaks for itself, her strategic vision, fearless advocacy, and proven ability to drive meaningful organizational and systemic change make her an invaluable addition to our Board of Trustees.”

Ms. Goss Graves is a nationally recognized expert on gender justice, law, policy, and culture change. As an attorney, she has spent her career fighting to advance opportunities for women and girls, including income security and COVID relief, equal pay, health and reproductive rights, education access, workplace justice and ending sexual harassment and violence – with a focus on women and girls of color. 

“Fatima Goss Graves possesses a sharp legal intellect, exceptional sector insight, and a steadfast dedication to justice,” said Heather Gerken, president of the Ford Foundation. “I could not be more excited to welcome her to the Board of Trustees. Across Fatima’s career, her strategic vision and formidable advocacy have broadened pathways for communities everywhere, particularly women and girls of color. Her presence and insights will be invaluable as we enter the next chapter of the Ford Foundation.”

“I am deeply honored to join the Board of Trustees and work alongside the Ford Foundation’s extraordinary leadership,” said Fatima Goss Graves. “I have dedicated my career to ensuring that all people can live with safety, dignity, and full agency over their lives and that women and their families have what they need to flourish. I am eager to bring that same commitment to Ford’s vital mission in the years ahead.”

Ms. Goss Graves has testified on complex policy matters at the state and federal levels of government in the United States and has been legal and social commentator on CBS, MSNBC, BBC, CNN, PBS, and NPR, and numerous outlets, including the New York Times, Wall Street Journal and the Washington Post. 

In addition to the Ford Foundation, Ms. Goss Graves serves on a number of boards in advisory and governance capacities. Based in Washington D.C., she is a graduate of UCLA and Yale Law School. 

Ford Foundation trustees are elected by the board and serve six-year terms. Trustees set broad policies relating to grantmaking, geographic focus, investments, governance, and professional standards, and they oversee independent audits. The foundation’s trustees come from around the world and have extensive experience in higher education, business and finance, technology, law, government, civil society, and the nonprofit sector.

Ursula Burns, Founder of Integrum, Chairwoman of Teneo, and Former CEO of Xerox Corporation, Elected as New Chair of the Ford Foundation Board of Trustees

item.title: Ford, MacArthur, and Robert Wood Johnson Foundations Announce First-of-Its-Kind Credit Union for People with Disabilities
item.description:
• News and press
  • |News

Artichoke Credit Union, designed with and for the disability community, will aim to increase financial inclusion for people with disabilities, who often face unique challenges in the financial services marketplace. 

NEW YORK – The Ford Foundation, the John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation, and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation (RWJF) today announced joint funding to launch a credit union to serve people with disabilities. Artichoke Credit Union is a sub-brand created in partnership with Michigan State University Federal Credit Union (MSUFCU) and is designed to center the needs, voices, and experiences of the disability community, with the goal of increasing financial inclusion for people with disabilities. 

Artichoke Credit Union, the first credit union of its kind, is designed to serve people with disabilities, their families, caregivers, advocates, and supporting organizations nationwide. Artichoke Credit Union is expected to begin accepting member sign-ups in the early second quarter of 2027.

The name Artichoke Credit Union is inspired by Ed Roberts, a pioneer in the independent living movement. When Roberts, who contracted polio at age 14, overheard a doctor tell his mother that he would be a “vegetable” if he survived the illness, Roberts declared that he “decided to be an artichoke—a little prickly on the outside but with a big heart.” Roberts was also the first MacArthur Fellow with a disability. 

The foundations, all of which are members of the President’s Council on Disability Inclusion in Philanthropy, are announcing the launch today at a Ford Foundation-led disability economic summit at Gallaudet University in Washington, D.C. 

“A thriving democracy depends on economic inclusion, yet millions of Americans with disabilities cannot access the financial tools needed to build assets and secure their independence,” said Heather Gerken, president of the Ford Foundation. “The Ford Foundation is proud to partner with the John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation, the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, and Michigan State University Federal Credit Union, to support Artichoke Credit Union. Artichoke Credit Union is designed by and for the disability community and exemplifies the structural changes needed to dismantle systemic barriers, expand access, and restore economic agency for every individual.”

“Artichoke Credit Union highlights what we can achieve when we prioritize disability inclusion,” said John Palfrey, president of the MacArthur Foundation. “When we listen to the disability community to understand their needs and incorporate their perspectives, we can build institutions that better serve everyone.”

“Health and financial well-being are inextricably linked. Achieving health equity is only possible if we work together to build a more inclusive economy,” said Richard Besser, MD, president and CEO of RWJF. “Artichoke Credit Union will help tear down persistent barriers to financial stability for people with disabilities, creating pathways for dignity, financial freedom, and, ultimately, better health.” 

The Ford Foundation partnered with Financial Health Network (FHN), a leading authority on financial health, to understand the feasibility of standing up a financial services organization, such as a credit union, specifically designed to serve people with disabilities. Research conducted by FHN found that the disability community faces numerous obstacles to financial inclusion, including banking services that fail to meet the needs of disabled people, high fees, limited access to low-cost credit, challenging asset limits, and low awareness in the financial sector of tools such as ABLE accounts. FHN’s research also found a lack of awareness of the diverse experiences and needs of people with disabilities and that most financial institutions are not courting the disability community as customers. 

Artichoke Credit Union is designed to help address these challenges through accessible banking, specialized financial education, responsible lending, inclusive product design, tools that support long-term financial well-being, and ongoing community-driven improvements. At launch, Artichoke Credit Union is expected to offer checking and savings accounts, certificates, personal loans, credit and debit cards, financial education resources, and budgeting tools. Members will also have access to support through live chat, phone, and video services, along with accessibility-focused features such as account alerts, guardian access options, and other custom-designed tools shaped by the needs of the community it serves.

MSUFCU is headquartered in East Lansing, Michigan, and has a long track record of building financial wellness for its members as a low-income designated credit union. A $5 membership share will establish membership with the credit union, and members will have access to support through live chat, phone, video services, and digital banking tools.

“The creation of Artichoke Credit Union is more than a new brand. It is an opportunity to listen, learn, and build alongside the disability community. Throughout our history, MSUFCU has embraced innovation to remove barriers and expand opportunity, from being among the first to offer accessible ATMs and supporting accessibility-focused lending programs to investing in innovative fintech solutions that create more inclusive experiences,” said April Clobes, president and CEO of MSUFCU. “As we serve more than 400,000 members, we remain committed to meeting each individual where they are and creating experiences that empower financial independence. We are proud to be the financial institution leading this initiative and further the credit union mission of making financial services more accessible, inclusive, and empowering for all.” 

The launch of Artichoke Credit Union is supported by two leaders of the disability rights movement: former senator Tom Harkin and former representative Tony Coelho, who were two of the primary Senate and House authors of the Americans With Disabilities Act (ADA). 

“In the 36 years since we passed the Americans With Disabilities Act, we have made tremendous progress when it comes to opening doors and breaking down physical barriers, but if a person with a disability cannot access the financial systems that fuel our economy, then the promise of full independence remains unfulfilled,” said Senator Tom Harkin. “True independence is not just about being able to physically get through the front door of a bank; it is about what you can do once you are inside, or when you log on to their app from home. When a banking website isn’t compatible with screen readers, or when a mobile payment app requires complex hand movements that are difficult to navigate, that is a modern-day barrier. That is exactly why a credit union dedicated to serving people with disabilities is so critically important. By providing accessible banking, fair lending, and financial literacy tailored to the community, Artichoke Credit Union is building an accessible digital workspace for people who just need a fair shot.”

“Economic justice for people with disabilities is part of the unfinished business of the ADA. For too long, issues like lack of accessibility and asset limits have restricted the potential for full economic inclusion and access to capital,” said Representative Tony Coelho. “Artichoke Credit Union addresses these challenges head-on by designing financial services in partnership with the disability community in order to serve a wide range of people with disabilities and their families. I am excited to support Artichoke Credit Union and look forward to becoming a proud member of the credit union when it launches next year.” 

Artichoke Credit Union is a trade name of MSUFCU, which is regulated by the National Credit Union Administration (NCUA). Deposits of up to $250,000 are federally insured.

item.title: The Stakes of America’s 2026 Midterm Elections
item.description:
• News and press
  • |In the press

Published in TIME

By Heather Gerken and Robert E. Rubin

Five years ago, in the wake of the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol, America’s civic institutions pledged to do more to defend our system of fair and free elections. Major philanthropies increased their investments in programs that defend democracy. Law firms expanded their pro bono election-protection work. University presidents publicly condemned the effort to thwart the will of American voters. Many of the country’s largest businesses pledged to stop donating to candidates who had tried to overturn an election.

Today, our elections are again under attack. But while some institutions have maintained their commitment to defending democracy, far too many have retreated.

item.title: Creativity and Free Expression
item.description:
The stories we tell, and the art we create, help us understand our world and make connections to others. Yet the stories we hear the most still disproportionately favor and represent a select few. By lifting up underrepresented or unheard voices, we can strengthen understandings of human complexity. We can push back against narratives that undermine fairness. And we can disrupt inequality.

Our work explores how cultural narratives affect and shape our reality, and how the arts, journalism, and film can contribute to fairer and more just societies. We are committed to strengthening diverse networks of cultural producers and decision makers. We seek to illuminate the root causes of injustice.

Across our work we prioritize support to artist-driven projects and organizations that include deep and meaningful engagement with communities.

What we don’t fund

We know nonprofit staff’s time is valuable, so we discourage using it to submit proposals that don’t fall within funding guidelines. In this spirit, we aim to be transparent about what our grantmaking does not support.

Our grantmaking does not support advocacy and commissioned projects, educational initiatives and student projects, film schools, journalism tools and technology, and awards, scholarships, and endowment funds.

item.title: Future of Work(ers)
item.description:
The nature of work is changing—and at a magnitude that we have yet to fully grasp, let alone respond to. Over the past several decades, the workplace has been transformed by globalization, changing power dynamics, and the growing economic role of financial markets. New and emerging technologies—including artificial intelligence, robotics, and big data—are playing an increasingly important role in shaping the jobs of the future, by shifting jobs between sectors, transforming the kinds of tasks that are done in existing jobs, and changing how people connect to work. Traditional employment is beginning to look more and more like “gig” work, with unpredictable work schedules and more precarious working conditions and rewards.

These changes have broad implications. As technological innovation upends more sectors of the economy—displacing jobs and changing the nature of work tasks—deep economic anxiety fuels mistrust of democratic institutions and magnifies age-old prejudices and discrimination. Labor market policies, which regulate and help determine the nature of employment and employer-worker arrangements, have not kept up. Millions of workers can’t afford to simply cope with a changing marketplace and growing economic risk.

Worldwide, many types of workers are affected by these seismic changes, from the creative professional working “gig to gig” to the retail or restaurant worker, the home care worker negotiating price and availability with customers through an app, the construction worker, and the long-haul trucker worried about a future of driverless vehicles. But the changes are not impacting people equally: women, people of color, migrants and people with disabilities disproportionately bear the brunt, exacerbating inequality overall.

If harnessed properly, new technologies have the potential to create new industries, occupations, and jobs. Rather than simply replacing human labor, technology can augment it. Tech can also be a boon to people with disabilities, and has the potential to help increase human productivity as well as job quality. Maximizing this potential will require strong policies, regulations, standards, and innovative business practices that increase quality work and economic security. It will mean building a broad coalition of workers and their advocates, the private sector, and policy makers across levels of government to generate ideas and promote action. And it will take leadership from robust organizations focused on amplifying the power of workers.

What we don’t fund

We know our partners’ time is valuable, so we discourage using it to submit proposals that don’t fall within funding guidelines. In this spirit, we aim to be transparent about what our grantmaking does not support.

We do not make grants to support efforts to strengthen economic and financial security outside the context of work for example in areas such food and nutrition assistance. We do not fund scientific or technological research that is disconnected from work and workers. And we do not fund workforce development and skill-building, or entrepreneurship training and financing.

Note: The foundation’s Mission Investments team does invest in enterprises, including funds that emphasize job quality.

It will mean building a broad coalition of workers and their advocates, the private sector, and policy makers across levels of government to generate ideas and promote action. And it will take leadership from robust organizations focused on amplifying the power of workers.

What we don’t fund

We know our partners’ time is valuable, so we discourage using it to submit proposals that don’t fall within funding guidelines. In this spirit, we aim to be transparent about what our grantmaking does not support.

We do not make grants to support efforts to strengthen economic and financial security outside the context of work for example in areas such food and nutrition assistance. We do not fund scientific or technological research that is disconnected from work and workers. And we do not fund workforce development and skill-building, or entrepreneurship training and financing.

Note: The foundation’s Mission Investments team does invest in enterprises, including funds that emphasize job quality.

item.title: Gender, Racial, and Ethnic Justice
item.description:
Despite significant progress, structural inequality based on gender, race, class, disability, and ethnicity persists around the world and is compounded and complicated by today’s challenges. Gender-based violence—rooted in patriarchy and laws, policies, and cultural norms aimed at curtailing rights—inflicts deep, lasting physical, psychological, and economic damage. People of color are disproportionately policed and incarcerated. Immigrants and LGBTQ+ people are targeted simply because of who they are.

But today’s realities have helped fuel vibrant new leaders and movements engaging in innovative advocacy and forging powerful alliances. In the Global South, there are efforts underway to reframe narratives to represent the experiences of women and girls around the world. In the United States, young people are leading new movements for immigrant rights and for racial justice that are challenging xenophobia, standing up for black lives, and interrogating the equation of police and prisons with community safety. Our work is to support the courageous people and organizations at the center of this fight to achieve lasting political and social change.”

We recognize that race, gender, class, disability, and ethnic identity are deeply connected—often inextricably so—and make sure our efforts are rooted in this understanding. It’s an understanding that informs our commitment to shifting repressive power dynamics and strengthening the rights and influence of those most affected by violence, oppression and injustice across the globe.

The Future is Hers

Around the world, women have become an unstoppable force.
They are rewriting the rules, redefining power, and reimagining what equality looks like.

item.title: Global Governance
item.description:
Today’s urgent problems include dangerously high levels of global inequality, shifting power dynamics among countries and regions, and ongoing crises such as climate change, pandemics, and migration. Managing these issues requires new systems of cooperation and the reimagining of international cooperation and governance to center those communities that are most deeply impacted by the very problems these systems were established to address.

Our goal is to help promote social justice and disrupt inequality within systems of global governance and international cooperation by bringing together diverse ideas, institutions, and individuals to advance a shared vision for achieving a just and inclusive global order. By fostering dialogue and strategic alliances among civil society, international non-governmental organizations, governments and intergovernmental organizations, we aim to promote democratic values, justice, and inclusivity as core principles in changing global governance systems.

Around the world, we seek to engage with critical stakeholders and partners in government, civil society, private sector and philanthropy to promote the idea of a global community with shared, concrete and cooperative problem-solving approaches and capabilities.

item.title: Mission Investments
item.description:
The Ford Foundation’s Mission Investments program launched in 2017 with the goal of making grants, program-related investments, and mission-related investments that improve how capitalism works for people. We support opportunities in the United States and the Global South, including Latin America, Africa, China, India, Indonesia, and the Middle East.

Our capital helps grow the impact investing sector, and our work creates a more inclusive form of capitalism and a more economically just world. We invest primarily in private equity and venture capital firms that address specific impact themes.

Mission-Related Investments

In 2017, Ford made a historic commitment to invest up to $1 billion of our endowment over a 10-year period in mission-related investments (MRIs) to address social problems while seeking risk-adjusted financial returns. In practice, we seek a level of financial returns required to sustain a perpetual foundation endowment.

Program-Related Investments

Since 1968, Ford has committed over $865 million in program-related investments (PRIs).  Today, the $350 million PRI Fund supports investment opportunities that meet IRS-qualifying charitable investment criteria, are catalytic and innovative in nature, and advance the foundation’s broad programmatic objectives.

Transcript

Accessibility Statement

  • All videos produced by the Ford Foundation since 2020 include captions and downloadable transcripts. For videos where visuals require additional understanding, we offer audio-described versions.
  • We are continuing to make videos produced prior to 2020 accessible.
  • Videos from third-party sources (those not produced by the Ford Foundation) may not have captions, accessible transcripts, or audio descriptions.
  • To improve accessibility beyond our site, we’ve created a free video accessibility WordPress plug-in.

Grants

Our grantmaking supports institutions, networks, and standards that encourage capital markets to work for, rather than against, our mission to promote human flourishing and address inequality.    

If you believe your organization, strategy, and proposal fit our criteria, you may submit your materials to [email protected]. Please note that we can only respond to those proposals that we believe meet our criteria.

item.title: Natural Resources and Climate Justice
item.description:
As the climate crisis escalates, the extraction of natural resources—such as oil, gas, minerals and forests— continues to dispossess and marginalize land-connected communities, driving inequality and injustice. Today, the race to mitigate climate change with rapid shifts to renewable energy, transition mineral extraction, and market-based forest protection strategies, for example, risks reproducing and deepening these same injustices by further exploiting communities whose rights are not secure.

There is clear global recognition that the decarbonization of energy systems and the protection of forests are essential in fighting climate change. Evidence shows that under many scenarios, ensuring that local communities have the power and security to manage their lands is an affordable and effective approach for forest and biodiversity conservation that improves community livelihoods. The transition away from fossil fuel-dependent energy systems and towards clean, sustainable models offers a unique chance to deliver justice for communities that have historically suffered harm rather than benefited from these systems. The viability of these transitions is also often enhanced when communities participate fully in their design and governance.

Our goal is to ensure that the priorities of historically disadvantaged communities and land-connected peoples from the Global South–including Indigenous Peoples, Afro-descendant peoples, and rural communities–are reflected in policies and practices to advance climate justice globally. 

We work to put the people most affected by climate injustice at the center of solutions by supporting efforts to strengthen the land tenure and resource rights of land-connected communities, advocating for energy transition processes that are fair and inclusive, strengthening the capacity of social movements and community organizations to press for their rights and influence policies, and engaging with government, civil society, research-based and private sector actors committed to these same goals.

item.title: Technology and Society
item.description:
Digital communications technologies have transformed how we connect and engage with the world around us, creating opportunities in every area of contemporary life. But as often as these technologies are used to foster learning and promote justice, they have also been used in ways that amplify inequality. Too many people—particularly those who have historically been excluded or marginalized—aren’t able to access, benefit from, or influence digital platforms. The governance and use of technology are implicated in nearly all the drivers of inequality, underscoring the extent of this problem.

We believe in equal access to, and fair regulation of, digital technology that is designed to advance transparency, privacy, access to knowledge, and free expression for all people. As the speed of global technological change and innovation outpaces public understanding and democratic checks—and as technology continues to reshape relationships between citizens, governments, civil society organizations, and corporations—our work focuses on protecting civil and human rights and freedom of expression.

To ensure that technology develops to meet the needs of the public, we support the growth of technically sophisticated, diverse organizations dedicated to advancing equitable and more inclusive digital spaces and systems. And we seek to develop the technological capacity of social justice organizations, key to strengthening the impact of their vital work in today’s environment.
